items.prompt: Putting all five nodes of the tiny graph on one side gives cutsize 0, so it is the best starting split.
items.explain: With every node on side 0 no edge is cut, so the cutsize is 0, but side 1 is empty. A legal start needs both sides non-empty and neither side above ceil(5/2) = 3 nodes.

items.prompt: The tiny graph has 5 nodes of size 1. Which split is a legal start (neither side above ceil(5/2) nodes)?
items.explain: ceil(5/2) = 3, so each side may hold at most 3 nodes. 5|0, 1|4 and 4|1 break the limit; 2|3 is the only legal shape.

items.prompt: Tiny graph: A–B 5, A–C 1, B–C 4, C–D 2, D–E 5, C–E 1. What is the cutsize of the split AB | CDE?
items.explain: Only A–C (1) and B–C (4) cross between {A, B} and {C, D, E}: 1 + 4 = 5.

items.prompt: Random start on the tiny graph, seeds 0 to 15. The cutsize you get ranges from…
items.explain: Seeds 5, 14 and 15 give ABC|DE with cut 3; seed 3 gives ACE|BD with cut 16. The same method on the same graph spans a wide range, so one random start is luck.

items.prompt: Grow starts at one node and adds the node reached by the heaviest edge until floor(5/2) = 2 nodes are in. Which start node gives the best split ABC | DE (cut 3)?
items.explain: Grow from D adds E (edge D–E, weight 5) and stops, leaving ABC | DE with cut 3. Grow from A or B gives AB | CDE (cut 5); grow from C gives ADE | BC (cut 9).

items.prompt: Star graph: A–B 9 and A to each of C, D, E, F with weight 5. The old greedy returns ABDEF | C with cut 5. The capped greedy returns ABD | CEF with cut 15. Which one is the better START for refinement?
choices: ABDEF | C, because 5 is smaller than 15
ABD | CEF, because ABDEF | C is not legal (5 | 1, cap is 3)
Neither: a start must have cut 0
items.explain: With 6 nodes the cap is ceil(6/2) = 3, so only 3|3 is legal. The 5|1 split has the smaller cut only because it cheats on balance. The lowest cut any 3|3 split can reach on this graph is 15.

items.prompt: Tie graph: A–B 5, A–E 3, B–F 3, C–D 1, D–E 5, E–F 1. The two heaviest edges tie at 5. Greedy anchored on A–B gives cut 9. Anchored on D–E, the cut is…
items.explain: Anchored on D–E, greedy ends with ABF | CDE. Only A–E (3) and E–F (1) cross, so the cut is 4. A tie in weight means the tie-break rule decides the answer: A–B gives 9, D–E gives 4.

items.prompt: Bridge graph (two triangles of weight 3, joined by C–D with weight 4): greedy gives cut 12 but growing from A gives cut 4. Building several starts and keeping the best legal one can beat any single method.
items.explain: Greedy anchors on the heaviest edge, which is the bridge C–D, so it mixes the two triangles (cut 12). Grow from A keeps the triangle ABC whole (cut 4). Trying greedy and every grow start and keeping the smallest cut finds 4.
